title: Lesson 1: Highway Development and Transportation Planning
description: From regional movement needs to precise geometric alignments.

content.text: Highway development progresses from Need (Macro) to Network, Corridor, and Facility (Micro). The goal is to identify and justify a transportation solution that serves a defined need.

items: Need: regional demand, connectivity gaps, and strategic goals.
Network: regional routes, intermodal connections, and capacity requirements.
Corridor: topographical, environmental, and land-use constraints within a right-of-way.
Facility: specific infrastructure elements, cross-sections, and material specifications.

content.text: The linear development chain is Need -> Planning -> Corridor -> Alignment -> Design -> Construction -> Operation. Information must support the next decision because weak early assumptions can cause expensive later design changes.

content.alt: Macro to micro infrastructure progression from need to facility
content.caption: Need -> Network -> Corridor -> Facility

items: Arterial: high mobility and speed, low property access, and movement between major activity centers.
Collector: gathers and distributes trips with moderate mobility and access.
Local: direct property access with low mobility and speed.

content.text: Networks contain nodes (trip start, end, or transfer points) and links (routes connecting nodes). Redundancy provides alternative paths when a link fails.

items: Radial: routes converge on a central hub.
Linear: movement follows a valley or coastline.
Ring + radial: a ring distributes radial traffic.
Irregular: responds to terrain or historic constraints.

content.alt: Mobility and access continuum showing arterial, collector, and local roads
content.caption: Functional road hierarchy
Grid, radial, linear, ring and radial, and irregular networks

content.text: The planning cycle is Problem -> Data -> Forecast -> Alternatives -> Evaluate -> Decide, centered on mobility, accessibility, safety, and sustainability.

items: Long-term: new strategic corridors responding to growth, changed travel patterns, and planned infrastructure.

content.text: Origin-destination studies show where trips begin and end and which zones interact. Thicker desire lines reveal corridors with concentrated movement demand.

content.caption: Problem -> Data -> Forecast -> Alternatives -> Evaluate -> Decide

content.alt: Existing and future conditions across short, medium, and long planning horizons
content.caption: Existing and future conditions

content.alt: Origin destination map with nodes and desire lines
content.caption: O-D desire lines reveal concentrated travel demand

content.text: Route selection considers terrain and geology, hydrology, right-of-way, cost and logistics, and environment. The physically shortest route is not automatically the best route.
Reconnaissance rapidly understands the corridor; preliminary survey compares alternatives; detailed survey supplies exact topography, utilities, and site details for geometric design.
GIS route optimization stacks O-D desire lines, land use and right-of-way, and topography and hydrology to identify a feasible route corridor.

content.alt: Route selection criteria surrounding a proposed alignment
content.caption: Route selection is a multi-criteria decision

content.alt: Comparison of reconnaissance, preliminary, and detailed survey stages
content.caption: Survey stages from concept to detailed design

content.alt: GIS layers converging into a feasible route corridor
content.caption: Demand and constraints converge on a feasible corridor

content.text: Alignment refines a feasible corridor into a three-dimensional path. Plan-view elements include tangents, curves, and intersections; profile elements include grades, crest curves, and sag curves.

items: Do not begin detailed geometric design before confirming the transportation need.
Do not ignore surrounding network effects.
Do not choose the physically shortest route without evaluating terrain, impacts, and other constraints.

content.text: There is no universally perfect route. The preferred alternative depends on project objectives and physical, social, environmental, and construction constraints.

content.alt: Three-dimensional road alignment showing tangents, curves, intersections, grades, crest curves, and sag curves
content.caption: Alignment geometry in plan and profile
